title: Chapter Five: The Drowned Land of Saeftinghe and the Shared Border
subtitle: Europe's Largest Saltwater Tidal Marshland

content.introduction: In the far southwest of the Netherlands lies the 'Drowned Land of Saeftinghe,' the largest saltwater tidal marshland in Europe, spanning 4,100 hectares. Here, the river becomes a poet, where ancient villages disappear underwater with every high tide and reemerge with every low tide, as if telling forgotten stories of floods and life.
content.cross_border_cooperation: Adjacent to it is the cross-border 'Hedwige-Prosper Polder' project, connecting Dutch and Belgian lands in unprecedented cooperation to protect the region from storms, returning 465 hectares of reclaimed land to tidal nature. This area has become a living ecological laboratory, where new mudflats form and shelter at least 75 pairs of endangered avocets.
content.dutch_wisdom: A Dutch proverb on honesty: 'Beter één vogel in de hand dan tien in de lucht' – A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. Here, the Dutch and Belgians were honest in choosing to preserve and protect these birds, preferring the real bird over theoretical plans, making this land a haven for life.
content.story: It is said that on quiet nights, fishermen can still hear the bells of sunken churches in Saeftinghe. Those villages swallowed by the river in floods of past centuries have today become fertile ground for birds, as if the river rebuilt life over the ruins of the past, immortalizing the memory of those who drowned with the river's honesty.
content.historical_context: The reclamation of these lands dates back to the Middle Ages, but the depoldering project, which began in the second decade of the 21st century, reflects a radical shift in Dutch philosophy from 'fighting water' to 'living with water.'
content.cultural_proverb: What the sea takes, it returns one day, but it returns it more beautiful.
